title: New Jersey Purges 6,600 Noncitizens From Voter Rolls After DMV Software Error
excerpt: Governor Mikie Sherrill says a glitch in the state's motor vehicle system automatically registered noncitizens to vote between 2023 and 2024, with nearly 400 casting ballots in past elections.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • New Jersey's DMV error registered 6,600 noncitizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024.
  • Fewer than 400 noncitizens voted, with no evidence of affecting election outcomes.
  • Governor Mikie Sherrill ordered the removal of these voters and initiated an investigation.
  • The incident fuels national debates on election integrity and potential voter ID laws.
  • A software error in New Jersey's Motor Vehicle Commission system registered roughly 6,600 noncitizens to vote between June 2023 and June 2024, despite applicants indicating they were not U.S. citizens.
  • Fewer than 400 of those registered actually cast ballots, spread across party lines and geographic areas, with no evidence any election outcome was affected.
  • Governor Mikie Sherrill ordered the removal of all erroneously registered voters and launched an investigation, blaming the failure on her predecessor's administration.
  • The disclosure intensifies a national debate over election integrity as congressional Republicans advance the SAVE America Act requiring proof of citizenship to vote.

New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill announced on Tuesday that her administration has removed approximately 6,600 noncitizens from the state's voter rolls after discovering they were improperly registered by a software error in the Motor Vehicle Commission's system. Nearly 400 of those individuals voted in elections, according to the governor's preliminary analysis.

The error occurred between June 2023 and June 2024, under the administration of former Governor Phil Murphy. Applicants for driver's licenses and state identification cards who answered "no" when asked whether they were U.S. citizens were registered to vote anyway due to the software glitch. New Jersey is among 23 states and the District of Columbia that allow noncitizens to hold driver's licenses.

How the Error Went Undetected

The vendor responsible for the motor vehicle system software was IDEMIA, a French company that provides identity verification services for government programs including TSA PreCheck and facial recognition systems. According to Sherrill, the Motor Vehicle Commission took a full year to fix the issue once discovered, and no one in the Murphy administration disclosed the problem publicly or took corrective action.

"It's unacceptable that the vendor released software with such a glaring error. It's unacceptable that the MVC took a year to get this issue fixed and it's unacceptable that no one in the previous administration brought this to light."

— Mikie Sherrill, Governor of New Jersey

Sherrill said her newly appointed MVC administrator, Rosalie Johnson, has begun the process of replacing IDEMIA with a new vendor, with the transition expected as soon as next year. The governor also hired independent firm CSG Law to investigate how the failure occurred and what safeguards were missed.

Scale and Political Fallout

The roughly 400 noncitizens who voted were registered as Democrats, Republicans, and unaffiliated voters, scattered across the state. New Jersey had 6,688,367 registered voters as of last month's primary election, making the erroneous registrations a fraction of the total electorate. Sherrill said there is no evidence any election outcomes were affected.

The disclosure arrives at a politically charged moment. Last week, President Donald Trump used a prime-time televised address to claim nearly 250,000 noncitizens were registered to vote across California, New Jersey, Nevada, and Pennsylvania. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin sent letters to those four states requesting voter roll reviews, asserting that New Jersey alone could have as many as 35,152 potential noncitizens on its rolls — a figure Sherrill said she has received no supporting evidence for.

White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson pointed to the New Jersey revelation as justification for the SAVE America Act, which would require states to submit voter rolls to a national database with citizenship information. The bill remains stalled in the Republican-led Congress despite Trump's support.

Broader Election Integrity Debate

The House is scheduled this week to vote on measures advancing elements of the SAVE America Act, including voter ID requirements attached to a congressional stock-trading ban and a blueprint for a standalone version of the legislation packaged with a defense authorization bill.

Sherrill, a former Navy pilot and federal prosecutor, pushed back on Trump's broader election fraud narrative even as she confirmed the error in her state. She called the president's credibility on election integrity "zero" and accused him of undermining faith in American elections for over a decade.

"I think that Donald Trump has done more to undermine free elections in this country than certainly anyone in my lifetime, including Vladimir Putin."

— Mikie Sherrill, Governor of New Jersey

A 2026 Bipartisan Policy Center report found no evidence that noncitizen voting has ever been significant enough to affect an election outcome. States routinely audit voter rolls, and sporadic cases of noncitizen voting are investigated and prosecuted.

What to Watch

The investigation by CSG Law will determine the full scope of the software failure and whether additional noncitizens were registered outside the June 2023 to June 2024 window. Congressional action on the SAVE America Act could accelerate as Republicans use the New Jersey case to build momentum for federal voter verification requirements. For Indian Americans and other immigrant communities in New Jersey, the incident raises questions about how automatic voter registration systems interact with noncitizen driver's license programs — and whether similar errors have gone undetected in other states.
